newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers push for Clinton sex harassment lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers push for Clinton sex harassment lawsuit.

text.p: Lawyers representing Paula Jones in her sex harassment lawsuit against President Bill Clinton urged a Little Rock judge on Tuesday to push ahead with the case despite Clinton's request that it be dismissed.

Gilbert Davis and Joseph Cammarata said their client has already waited for more than three years to have her case heard, and that Clinton's lawyers were trying to "short circuit" the litigation with procedural manoeuvres.

In a 99-page filing to U.S. District Judge Susan Webber Wright, they said Clinton used his position as Arkansas governor to try to pressure Jones to agree to his request for sex at a Little Rock hotel in May 1991.

"The alleged actions of Mr. Clinton and his agents are not merely shocking: they are also clear abuses of power conferred upon Mr. Clinton as an official of the State of Arkansas," the attorneys said.
Earlier this month, Clinton's lawyers flatly denied all Jones' allegations and asked Judge Wright to postpone the discovery process in the case until she ruled on the dismissal motion.

Jones, a state employee while Clinton was governor, claims she was told by a state trooper to go to a hotel room to meet Clinton during a government conference and that Clinton exposed himself to her inside the room, asking her for oral sex.
Her lawyers said on Tuesday that Clinton and the state trooper repeatedly reminded Jones that Clinton was her ultimate boss, placing pressure on her to accept his request for sex.
They said Jones refused so Clinton again reminded her of his position and admonished her to keep quiet about the incident.

In his response to the lawsuit, Clinton earlier this month "adamantly" denied all the charges, saying Jones was motivated by greed and was collaborating with his political enemies in an attempt to damage his presidency.
Clinton's lawyers have tried to postpone the lawsuit until after he leaves the White House, arguing that it would distract him from his presidential duties.
But, in a landmark ruling, the Supreme Court said in May that Jones' lawsuit could proceed immediately.
Clinton has until Aug. 15 to reply to Jones' written arguments presented on Tuesday.
